description: Team Mission: Vesta, competing in Chicago on the Martian Map challenge. We're building Vesta Scout: a helicopter scouts the terrain ahead of an astronaut on Mars, and the app plans a safe walk with a way back to the habitat, using NASA Mars data. Our team is already formed in person; this page is for our members to join.
summary:
Would you walk a route on Mars that nobody has checked?

Mission Vesta is a map that plans safe science walks for the first astronauts on Mars. It runs in a desktop browser.

It turns NASA data into a 3D map of a real 2 x 2 km area of Gale crater. Every 8 m square knows its slope, its ground, its science value and the energy it takes to get home.

Orbit cannot see the rocks under about 1 m that stop a walk, so a helicopter scout flies the route first. It is modelled on NASA's planned SkyFall helicopters, and the app plans a new route after every landing.

In our test, three simulated flights took the route from 6 patches of rock to 0, with the same five science stops, for 1.5% more walking energy.

During the walk, the phone shows how far the astronaut can still go and get home. Every walk adds to the map for the next one.

It answers the challenge directly: one layered map, built from several NASA missions, that helps explorers do new science and come home safely.

Try it: https://nasa.nicolasrufino.com/scout
details:
Would you walk a route on Mars that nobody has checked?

Mission Vesta is a map that plans a safe science walk for astronauts on Mars. A helicopter checks the route before anyone steps outside.

The problem

  • Mars maps are flat. They are made from orbit, so they do not show what stops a person on foot.
  • What stops a walk is small. NASA sets 20° as the steepest slope an astronaut in a suit can walk, and 30 cm as the highest step.
  • Orbit cannot see small rocks. Rocks under about 1 m are missing from the map, but they block the way.
  • It has already happened. In NASA's 2022 moonwalk rehearsal in Arizona (JETT3), slopes steeper than the suit allows stopped the crew from reaching their most important science stop.
  • Nobody can help live. A message from Mars takes 3 to 22 minutes to reach Earth, so the plan must be right before the walk starts.

What Mission Vesta does

Mission Vesta is a web app, built for a desktop browser in landscape view (it may not work as well on a phone). It shows a real 2 x 2 km area of Gale crater on Mars, where the Curiosity rover studied ridges left by ancient water. It works in five steps.

  1. Orbit. We turn NASA's flat images into a 3D map of the ground. The map has 65,536 squares, each 8 m wide. Every square knows its slope, its ground, its science value and the energy it takes to get home.
  2. Scout. A helicopter flies the route and finds the rocks that orbit missed. After every landing, the app plans a new route around them.
  3. Plan and pack. The app works out the effort, the time, the way home and the best order for the stops, before anyone leaves.
  4. Walk and add. The phone shows how far the astronaut can still go and get home. At each stop, it lists the tasks and saves the readings to the map.
  5. Repeat. The crew scouts one sol (one Mars day) and walks the next. Every walk starts from a map that knows more.

What the helicopter carries, and what our map does with it

NASA is already building the helicopters: the SkyFall mission, planned for late 2028. They carry all of the instruments below, and we change nothing on them. We built the software that turns what they see into a safe route.

  • Colour cameras see rocks and ledges that are too small to see from orbit. Our map blocks those squares and plans a new route. This is built. The flights are simulated: a NASA 25 cm image from orbit stands in for the helicopter's camera.
  • Near-infrared cameras see which minerals are on the surface. Our map scores how much science each square holds. This is built, using mineral data from orbit (CRISM).
  • A dosimeter and air sensors measure radiation and temperature along the route. Our map shows the conditions for the walk. This is built, using Curiosity's RAD and REMS readings.
  • Ground radar sees deep sand or ice, 3 to 5 m under the surface. Our map will use it to warn about ground that only looks solid. This is not built yet, because there is no radar data for this site.

One walk, start to finish

  1. The crew picks five science stops that Curiosity visited.
  2. The app plans a route from orbit data alone. It is 1,275 m long, and it crosses 6 patches of rock that orbit cannot see.
  3. The helicopter checks the route in three flights.
  4. The app plans a new route. It crosses 0 patches of rock, with the same five stops, for 1.5% more walking energy.
  5. The walk uses 630 of the 1,266 kJ of energy the astronaut can spend. Half is left for detours and surprises, and the emergency reserve stays full.

Impact for NASA

  • About 30 times cheaper. A helicopter scout costs about 30 times less than a rover. Ingenuity cost about $85M, and Curiosity cost $2.5B.
  • 77 times faster. Curiosity needed 154 sols to reach five science stops. A crew needs 2 sols: one to scout the route and one to walk it.
  • More science per mission. A crew can do up to 15 walks in a 30-sol stay, with five stops each. That is 75 stops.
  • Safer crews. The helicopter meets the hazards first. The crew decides in the habitat, not in the middle of a walk.

How we checked it

  • The ground is right. Curiosity measured its height at 148 points as it drove. Our map agrees within 12 cm on average.
  • The science finder works. We tested it on 90 places Curiosity drove. It ranks a place with ridges above a place without them 85% of the time. It also found 8 places no rover has visited.
  • The rocks are real. JPL's ROSCO rock detector proposed 25 rocks at our site, and a person confirmed 23 of them.
  • Anyone can repeat it. Every number on this page comes from a script in our public repository: https://github.com/nicolasrufino/nasaspaceapps

How it works

  • Walking energy. We use the Pandolf equation (75 kg body, 60 kg suit and kit), scaled for Mars gravity. Sand costs 2.4 times more than rock.
  • Blocked ground. A slope over 20° or a step over 30 cm is a wall, from NASA's suit limits.
  • The way home. Dijkstra's algorithm finds the cheapest way home from every square, once. The phone only looks the answer up, so it needs no link to Earth.
  • Stop order. The Held-Karp algorithm finds the best order, exact up to 12 stops.
  • Scouting. Fly, land and plan again is a known problem: the Canadian Traveller Problem with remote sensing (Bnaya, Felner and Shimony, 2009).
  • Rocks. ROSCO finds rocks by their shadows in a 25 cm HiRISE image.

What makes it creative

  • The map grows. The helicopter corrects it before the walk, the astronaut adds to it during the walk, and the next walk starts from both.
  • Every route starts from the way home. The app plans how to get back, not only how to get there.

What is simulated

  • The helicopter flights are simulated. The scout reveals a stored hazard layer built from NASA data. No sensor is simulated.
  • Zero rocks on the route means zero in our stored hazard layer. It does not mean the route is verified safe on Mars.
  • Our terrain classifier is 92–94% right on Curiosity photos and 73% on Perseverance photos from a crater it never saw, so it does not steer the route.
  • The energy budget and the Mars gravity factor (0.68) are estimates, and the app marks them as estimates.

Built with

  • JavaScript, three.js and Vite, for the app.
  • Python with GDAL, for the NASA data pipeline.
  • PyTorch exported to ONNX, with ONNX Runtime Web, for the terrain classifier.
  • Node.js and Playwright, for the numbers and the tests.
  • GitHub Actions and Azure Static Web Apps, for hosting.

Use of AI

We used AI coding assistants (Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex) for coding, debugging, research, data analysis and writing, including drafting this text.

Team Mission: Vesta (Chicago)

  • Jules: scout, measurements and machine learning.
  • Nicolas: 3D app and terrain.
  • Luca: NASA data pipeline, world integration and hazard views.
  • Galsan: submission, project page and release.
